questions.question: What parts of the human ear are caused to vibrate by incoming sound waves?
options: Only the outer ear flap and the ear canal
The eardrums, the tiny bones within our ears, and the cochlea
Just the brain and the auditory nerve
The vocal cords and the throat muscles

questions.question: Where in the human ear are the specialised cells that sense vibrations and send electrical signals to the brain?
options: The outer ear
The eardrum
The cochlea
The middle ear bones

questions.question: How does the brain create the sensation of hearing a sound?
options: By receiving physical vibrations directly from the skull bones
By detecting changes in blood pressure in the inner ear
By receiving electrical signals from the ear through a nerve
By sending sound waves back out into the ear canal

questions.question: What is the typical frequency range of sound waves that a human ear can detect?
options: 20 Hz to 20 kHz
2 Hz to 200 Hz
200 kHz to 20 MHz
50 Hz to 50 kHz

questions.question: How are sound waves originally created by an object?
options: The object heats up, causing radiation to spread through space
The object vibrates, causing nearby air particles to vibrate too
The object absorbs light, releasing electrical charges
The object moves in a straight line at a constant speed

questions.question: When a sound wave travels through the air, how do the air particles move?
options: They travel all the way from the sound source to the listener's ear
They move in circular loops in the direction of the wave
They vibrate parallel to the direction of wave travel, without travelling forwards
They remain completely still and do not vibrate at all

questions.question: What type of wave is sound, and how do its vibrations relate to the direction of energy transfer?
options: Transverse wave, vibrating at 90 degrees to energy transfer
Longitudinal wave, vibrating parallel to energy transfer
Electromagnetic wave, vibrating in all directions
Circular wave, vibrating only in a clockwise direction

questions.question: Why does sound travel faster in solid materials than in liquids?
options: Solids have weaker forces between particles, allowing particles to move more freely
Solids have strong forces between particles, which helps vibrations travel even faster
Solids are less dense than liquids, so waves have less resistance
Solid particles are much larger and heavier than liquid particles

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the speed of sound in different media?
options: It is fastest in air (around 340 m/s), slower in liquids, and slowest in solids
It is about 340 m/s in air, faster in liquids, and faster still in solids
It is the same speed in air, liquids, and solids
It is about 300,000,000 m/s in air and slower in solids

questions.question: How can the speed of a sound wave be calculated?
options: speed = distance ÷ time
speed = distance × time
speed = time ÷ distance
speed = distance + time

questions.question: In an experiment to measure the speed of sound, why is it beneficial to measure longer distances and times?
options: It makes the sound wave travel much faster through the air
It ensures that any measurement errors are a smaller proportion of the results
It prevents the sound wave from reflecting off nearby surfaces
It increases the frequency of the sound waves produced

questions.question: How does ultrasound produce images of structures inside the human body?
options: It heats up tissues until they glow in the dark
It reflects from the boundaries between different tissues
It passes straight through all tissues without any change
It destroys the outer layer of tissue to reveal the inner layer

questions.question: Why are water waves classified as transverse waves?
options: Because the direction of oscillation is parallel to the direction of energy transfer
Because the direction of oscillation is 90° to the direction of energy transfer
Because they can travel through a vacuum without any particles
Because they can only travel in one direction and never reflect

questions.question: What is meant by the amplitude of a water wave?
options: The total distance a wave travels in one minute
The number of complete waves that pass a point each second
The greatest distance water moves above and below the rest position
The distance from one wave crest to the very next wave crest

questions.question: What is wave superposition?
options: The process of waves speeding up when they enter shallower water
The effect of waves adding up or cancelling out when they pass through each other
The absorption of wave energy by a soft barrier
The separation of a wave into its different frequency components
